newsitem.title: USA: Report sees 37 vulnerable U.S. nuclear plants.
newsitem.headline: Report sees 37 vulnerable U.S. nuclear plants.

text.p: Thirty-seven nuclear power plants representing 40 percent of U.S. nuclear generating capacity may be vulnerable to shut-down as the electricity market becomes less regulated, according to a study released Tuesday by the INGAA Foundation.

If all 37 sites closed, the report prepared by the Washington International Energy Group said that could open opportunities for up to 1.55 trillion cubic feet (tcf) of natural gas use per year in electricity generation.

That would be equivalent for about 45 percent of the natgas used for electricity generation in 1995, but the report said increased demand actually would be lower because improved efficiency in the electric industy would reduce the need for one-to-one replacement.
Most of the potential nuclear shutdowns would be in the Northeast and Midwest, where the report saw 1.16 tcf of total natgas potential.
The gas industry foundation said it commissioned the study as part of its effort to evaluate potential markets for natural gas.

The report looked at the economic performance of 71 nuclear sites, and looked at external forces such as license renewal, availability of a permanent waste disposal facility and stranded cost recovery.
Of the 71 sites, 34 were projected to be competitive as market prices should be at least as high as their operating costs. The remaining 37 sites were not projected to be competitive in 2005.
Vulnerable sites tended to be those with less capacity.
The report said some regions would be heavily affected by potential shutdowns.
For example, it said all six operating nuclear sites in New York were vulnerable, as well as all seven sights in the region of Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, western Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
In the region of Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska and the Dakotas, four sites with about 60 percent of total nuclear generation were vulnerable.
In the Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey and most of Pennsylvania region, four sites or about 47 percent of capacity were vulnerable.

In New England, it said four sites with about 51 percent of the capacity were vulnerable, and in Illinois, northern and eastern Wisconsin and eastern Missouri, five sets with 45 percent of capacity were vulnerable.
